messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi is a forty-two-year-old tax inspector who lives with his wife and two children in a quiet suburban neighborhood. He came to therapy reluctantly, at his wife’s insistence, after months of what she described as him “disappearing into himself.” On the PCL-5, his score was 72, and the story that emerged over the first sessions was one of a man haunted by a single moment he cannot undo.

Eighteen months ago, Ravi was driving home from a routine field audit on a two-lane road. He glanced down at his phone for a second—to check a message from his supervisor about a file he’d left on his desk—and when he looked up, a motorcycle had stopped in front of him to turn left. He hit the brakes too late. The impact threw the rider into the oncoming lane. Ravi remembers the sound of the helmet cracking against the asphalt, and the way the rider’s leg was bent at an angle that did not look like a leg anymore. He got out of his car and ran to the man, who was still conscious. The man looked up at him and said, “Please, I have kids.” Ravi held his hand until the ambulance came. The man survived, but with a traumatic brain injury and permanent paralysis from the waist down. Ravi was not charged; the police report noted the motorcycle had no functioning brake light. But that detail never mattered to Ravi. What mattered was that he had looked at his phone. He had failed to protect someone who trusted the road to be safe.

Since that day, Ravi has been unable to drive past any intersection where a car is waiting to turn left. His heart pounds when he sees a motorcycle, even in a parking lot. He takes back roads to work now, adding forty minutes to his commute, because the highway has too many cars stopped in turning lanes. At his desk, he finds himself staring at the ceiling, hearing the crack of the helmet over and over. The sound comes without warning—when a coworker drops a stapler, when a child’s bicycle skids on the sidewalk outside his window. He has learned to flinch before he even knows why.

What frightens Ravi most is the way the memory comes apart. Some moments are impossibly clear: the rider’s eyes, the angle of the leg, the exact words of the apology he stammered while kneeling on the asphalt. But the seconds before the impact are gone. He has tried to remember the color of the sky, the song on the radio, the feel of the steering wheel in his hands—and there is nothing. He feels like he is only holding fragments of the worst moment of his life, and the gaps terrify him because he cannot be sure what he missed, what he might have done differently if he had been paying more attention to the right thing. His mind tries to fill the blanks with worse possibilities: What if the man had died? What if his children were in the car behind him? What if the man’s wife blames him every day?

Ravi has come to believe that he should be punished. He tells himself he deserves to suffer, that the man’s paralysis is a weight he must carry for the rest of his life. Sometimes he catches himself thinking, “At least he didn’t die,” and then immediately feels sick—because comparing downward, reminding himself it could have been worse, feels like a betrayal of the man’s suffering. He tries not to think about the event at all. He has stopped watching news reports of accidents, stopped attending the annual memorial service for a colleague’s father, stopped going to funerals altogether. When his own mother called to say a distant uncle had died, Ravi made an excuse and did not go to the burial. He could not stand the sight of the grave, the way it would remind him of what he almost caused.

At work, he has become brittle. A junior inspector asked him once, casually, “Ever been in a bad accident?” and Ravi walked out of the room without answering. He now eats lunch alone in his car, with the windows rolled up, radio off, just staring at the dashboard. His supervisor has noticed that he avoids any case file involving motor vehicle collisions, and Ravi has started requesting only property tax assessments—boring, safe, nothing that touches people’s bodies. He knows this is costing him opportunities for promotion, but he cannot bring himself to care. What he cares about is the moment when a memory hits and he hears the rider’s voice again, and he feels the shame of having been the one who caused it. He feels permanently humiliated, as though he is marked by what he did. His belief that the world is a place where careful people can keep others safe has been destroyed. He used to think he was a good driver, a good father, a good man. Now he knows he is the kind of person who looks at his phone and ruins a stranger’s life.

What finally brought Ravi to therapy was a panic attack in his own driveway. He was backing out to pick up his son from school, and a neighbor’s child rode past on a bicycle. Ravi slammed the brakes, sat shaking in the driver’s seat, and could not move for ten minutes. His son was late to pickup. The school called his wife. That night, she told him, quietly, that she was scared for him. Ravi is not sure what he hopes for. He is afraid that talking about the event will make the memories worse, that he will lose even more of what little he remembers. But he is also afraid of staying the way he is—a man who cannot drive his own child to school, who cannot look at a grave, who cannot forgive himself for a moment that lasted less than two seconds.
